destination.title: Foundations
destination.why: A simple framework for growing as an engineer. A handful of capabilities, each climbed one rung at a time. A rung is finished when you can show it, not when you've read about it.

throughout.title: Build and test setup
items: CMake, multi-target
Catch2 or doctest
Google Benchmark
AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer on every build
ThreadSanitizer in CI from the day a thread exists
gdb and lldb, including reading core dumps
CI on every push
Compiler Explorer, opened as a reflex

throughout.title: Measurement
items: Predict the cost before measuring it
One variable per benchmark
DoNotOptimize and ClobberMemory, so the compiler cannot elide the work
Never a speedup without a variance figure, and never a mean alone
Microbenchmarks built per project, against that project's own seams

throughout.title: Problem practice
items: One problem a day into the solve log, half a page of notes per non-trivial one
Thirty minutes minimum before opening an editorial; read only enough to unblock, then finish it yourself
Every non-trivial algorithm stress-tested against a slow brute force with a random input generator
The STL when the clock is running; your own implementations only to understand them
Every dynamic programming recurrence written as one mathematical line before any code
Every two weeks: four problems from a past Div 3 round, two hours, no aids

reading: The live step is the lowest one whose finish line isn't met yet. All seven capabilities have one at once.
When capabilities compete for a slot: algorithms first, then C++, then the pricer, then performance, then concurrency, then design and systems together.
The first five decide whether the work holds up. Design and systems make it better once it does.

do: Wake at the same time. Every day, no exceptions.

do.text: One focus block on a live step. When two compete, the higher one wins.
do.note: If a weekday block goes flat: the next chapter of Kernighan & Pike, with notes.

do: Train: {training}. Then ten minutes of mobility.
One problem into the solve log, half a page of notes if it was non-trivial.
Money Stuff, and a little news.
The phone charges outside the bedroom. No screens in the final hour.
Read before bed, ten minutes at least.
Seven and a half hours in bed, at least.

protocol.never: No drinking, no smoking, no gooning, no dooming, no scrolling.
never_how: Zero, not less. Zero needs no decision.
Remove the access; don't resist the urge.

week.text: The Sunday sync: count the week, set the next.

month: Takeaway two or three times, no more.

split.Mon: Lower A, squat focus, plus a finisher
split.Tue: Upper A, horizontal push and pull, plus a finisher
split.Thu: Lower B, hinge focus, plus a finisher
split.Fri: Upper B, vertical push and pull, plus a finisher
split.Sun: Arms, wrists, forearms and grip, twice a month

rules: Main lift 4 sets of 4 to 6 at RPE 7 to 8. Accessories 3 sets of 8 to 12 at RPE 8. Hit the top of the range on every set, then add weight next session.
Finishers: 8 to 10 minutes, after lifting. Carries and rower on upper days, bike or sled on lower days.
Tibialis raises and the single-leg calf eccentric in every lower session.
Ten minutes of mobility after every session: front rack, thoracic, ankles.
Wednesday VO2: 4 × 4 minutes at 180–190 bpm, 3 minutes easy between, 10 minutes warm-up, 5 minutes cool-down. Don't stack fatigue into it on Tuesday.
Deload every sixth week: same sessions, 60% of the weight, full reps.

150 ml unsweetened oat milk, 80 g 2% Greek yogurt, 100 g frozen berries, 50 g frozen banana, 10 g ground flax, 30 g protein powder.

recovery: A missed day costs one day. It costs the plan nothing. You return the next morning at the same wake time.
No debt, no catch-up. Nothing carries between days.
No replanning. Setting what this week should prove is fine; rebuilding the roadmap isn't.

works.about: Each piece is a small tool plus a writeup: one sharp finding, and one named regime where the finding does not apply. One every six to eight weeks. The next one is whichever the live work has made cheapest.

shipped.name: mc754
shipped.what: Where Monte Carlo diverges from the analytic limit because of float arithmetic rather than sample variance, and where Kahan summation pays for itself.

shipped.name: atomic-probe
shipped.what: Which std::atomic operations actually compile to lock-free instructions, and the roughly 40× cost of the silent-lock path under contention.

shipped.name: detreduce
shipped.what: A reduction that gives bit-identical results regardless of thread count, topology or scheduling, and where that is required versus superstition.

shipped.name: linecache
shipped.what: Cross-architecture cache-line detection; 64-byte alignment is silently wrong on Apple Silicon, where L1 lines are 128 bytes.

shipped.name: cholupd
shipped.what: A streaming covariance estimator with an incrementally updated Cholesky factor, and the regimes where rounding breaks it.

queue.name: mc754-paths
queue.what: How rounding accumulates along a simulated path, and what it does to a path-dependent price.
queue.rides: Floating point line and pricer step 1

queue.name: isbetray
queue.what: When importance sampling increases variance instead of reducing it, and the condition that predicts it.

queue.name: vectranscend
queue.what: Vectorised exp and log in the per-path loop, accuracy against throughput.

queue.name: linecache-false
queue.what: Detecting false sharing from performance counters rather than inspection.

capabilities.name: Algorithms and problem-solving
capabilities.goal: Solve any DSA problem correctly, optimally, and in good time.
capabilities.why: Most hard problems are data-structure and algorithm problems underneath. Seeing the recurrence, the invariant and the cost quickly makes everything else faster to build and easier to trust.
capabilities.now: Erickson Ch 1 exercises and Kleinberg & Tardos Ch 5 to §5.5. The thirty recurrences and the five proofs.
continuous: Antti Laaksonen, Guide to Competitive Programming, as a companion reference

rungs.title: Analysis
rungs.because: First, because every later rung needs you to write a bound and a correctness argument.
items: Erickson, Algorithms, Ch 1 (recursion), paired with Kleinberg & Tardos, Algorithm Design, Ch 5 (divide and conquer)
Kleinberg & Tardos Ch 1–2: stable matching as a proof masterclass, and asymptotics
Thirty recurrences by hand: substitution, recursion tree, master theorem
Correctness and runtime proofs for binary search, mergesort, quickselect, BFS and Dijkstra
CSES Introductory, all eighteen
rungs.done_when: The recurrence and master-theorem case sketched on sight from a single editorial line, and the eighteen logged.

rungs.title: Containers, built from scratch
rungs.because: Second, because the hash map is the hardest check here and takes the longest to build. It doesn't depend on rung 3, so it shouldn't wait behind it.
items: Each unit-tested, stress-tested against the std:: equivalent, and microbenchmarked
byo::vector (amortised O(1) push, proof written), byo::list (correct iterator invalidation), byo::deque (segmented)
byo::stack, byo::queue, byo::priority_queue, byo::bitset
byo::hash_map last: chaining and Robin Hood, against adversarial hash inputs
Then mergesort, quicksort (median of three), heapsort, introsort, radix and counting sort, benchmarked on those containers
At the hash map, not before: Knuth, TAOCP Vol 3 §6.4; Celis, Robin Hood Hashing; Abseil's Swiss Tables notes and Kulukundis's CppCon 2017 talk; benchmark against absl::flat_hash_map
Alongside: CSES Sorting and Searching, core then extended
rungs.done_when: A hash map written from a blank file in under 30 minutes that survives 10⁷ adversarial operations.

rungs.title: Paradigms
rungs.because: After rung 1, because dynamic programming is recursion plus memoisation. Rungs 3 and 4 can be taken in either order.
items: Erickson Ch 2 backtracking, Ch 4 greedy
Erickson Ch 3 dynamic programming, with its exercises: the largest single item here
Kleinberg & Tardos Ch 4 (greedy, with the matroid framing) and Ch 6 (dynamic programming)
A memoisation framework: decorator for recursive, builder for iterative
A disjoint-set union with path compression, union by rank and rollback
CSES Dynamic Programming, core then advanced; AtCoder Educational DP, full set
Codeforces greedy tag 1400→1800, dp tag 1400→1900
rungs.done_when: A 1400 solved cold in 25 minutes three separate times, then a 1700 three times, and a 1700 classified within two minutes as greedy with an exchange argument, DP on subsequences, or divide and conquer on a dimension.

rungs.title: Graphs, the basics
items: Erickson Ch 5–8: basics, DFS, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
Kleinberg & Tardos Ch 3
byo::graph: adjacency lists, one iterator for directed and undirected
BFS, iterative DFS, Dijkstra on your own heap, Bellman-Ford, topological sort, Kruskal on your own DSU, Prim
CSES Graph Algorithms, from Counting Rooms to Cycle Finding
rungs.done_when: Dijkstra written from a blank file in under 10 minutes.

capabilities.name: C++
capabilities.goal: Real mastery of C++ across its history: what C++98/03 was like, what each standard changed, and why.
capabilities.why: The language everything else here is written in. Knowing exactly what each line does (copies, moves, lifetimes, what the compiler generates) is the difference between code that works and code you can reason about.
capabilities.now: Starts Wednesday 30 September: Meyers, Effective Modern C++, Items 1–4, then 18–22 on Friday.
capabilities.method: Every rung is organised by topic, walked from old to new: the old-language problem, the idiom that worked around it, what the committee changed and in which standard, why, and what is still rough.
continuous: The evolution log: one entry per feature met in rungs 1–3, with the old problem, the old idiom, what changed and when, the committee's reasoning, the proposal paper, and what is still rough. Finished when it covers every feature in rungs 1–3.
History: Stroustrup's HOPL III and HOPL IV papers, The Design and Evolution of C++, Sutter's trip reports, the proposals via wg21.link (for moves, N1377 and N2027)
Compiler Explorer as a reflex; sanitizers on every build
Carruth, Efficiency with Algorithms, Performance with Data Structures

rungs.title: Value semantics and ownership, old to new
rungs.because: First, because the containers and the pricer's core are written against it.
items: The old life: Meyers, Effective C++ 3rd ed, Items 5–25; Sutter, Exceptional C++, the exception-safety and class-design items (the three guarantees, copy-and-swap, Pimpl)
The change: Josuttis, C++ Move Semantics – The Complete Guide
The rules: Meyers, Effective Modern C++, Items 14 and 17–30, read after Josuttis as the checklist
Godbolt, What Has My Compiler Done for Me Lately?, then your own loop in Compiler Explorer on x86-64 and ARM64
rungs.done_when: Given any function signature, say what happens to each argument (copied, moved, elided, dangling) and why; and explain why auto_ptr was removed, why the rule of three became the rules of five and zero, and what C++17's guaranteed copy elision changed.

rungs.title: Generic code and lambdas, old to new
rungs.because: After rung 1, because templates are unreadable without value categories and forwarding.
items: Mechanics: C++ Templates: The Complete Guide, Ch 1–2 and 5 (two-phase lookup, dependent names, typename and template disambiguators)
Deduction: Effective Modern C++, Items 1–4
The four eras of constraining a template: C++03 traits and tag dispatch, C++11 enable_if and SFINAE, C++17 if constexpr, CTAD and folds, C++20 concepts
Non-type template parameters, old to new
Lambdas across the standards: functors and bind, then C++11, 14, 17 and 20; Meyers Items 31–34
rungs.done_when: One generic component written three ways (C++03 traits, C++11 SFINAE, C++20 concepts), all three compiling to the same code in Compiler Explorer, and you can say what each step fixed.

rungs.title: The rest of modern C++
rungs.because: After rung 2, because most of it is generic code underneath.
items: C++17 vocabulary: optional, variant, string_view, structured bindings
C++20: the spaceship operator, ranges and views, consteval and constinit (with Meyers Item 15), designated initialisers; coroutines and modules at the level of the problem each solves
Source: Josuttis's C++17 and C++20 guides
rungs.done_when: For each feature, state the workaround it replaced and show both in a small example.

rungs.title: How the standard library does it
rungs.because: After rung 3, because the source is template-heavy and uses the whole modern language.
items: libc++, one question per component
vector: how growth stays exception-safe when elements move
shared_ptr: the control block, and why make_shared is one allocation
function: type erasure and the small-buffer optimisation
sort: where introsort's thresholds are, and why
rungs.done_when: Each answer explained, with what a naive version gets wrong.

capabilities.name: Probability, numerics and the pricer
capabilities.goal: Probability sharp enough to solve unfamiliar problems cold, and a pricer that proves you understand the numerics behind it.
capabilities.why: Reasoning under uncertainty, and numerics you can trust. The pricer is where both are proven: every result checked against a known answer, with its error stated.
capabilities.now: Pricer: the validation harness. Probability: Blitzstein & Hwang Ch 1–2.

rungs.title: The pricer
rungs.because: In dependency order. The pricer ranks third of everything: every later step waits on the harness.
items: 1 Validation harness: closed-form Black–Scholes separate from the Monte Carlo path, agreement to a stated tolerance, convergence at the expected rate, a standard error on every price. Reading: the floating point line; Hull on options, binomial trees, Itô and Black–Scholes–Merton
2 Naive baseline, tagged and locked, with machine, flags and turbo state recorded
3 Three independent seams: product, model, RNG. Reading: Joshi Ch 1–9; take the decomposition, use templates where he uses inheritance

4 Variance reduction and quasi-Monte Carlo (Sobol with Brownian bridge). Reading: Glasserman Ch 1–2, 4–5; derive the control-variate coefficient, the antithetic condition, and why Sobol only wins at low effective dimension
5 Reverse-mode AAD: price and full sensitivities in one pass. Reading: Savine; derive pathwise delta and the likelihood-ratio estimator
6 Desk layer: implied vol solver, curve bootstrapped from instruments, surface fitted to quotes

Design commitments from the first line: core templated on scalar type; exactly one type-erased boundary, at the factory rim; the per-path loop fully static and inlined; a new product is one new file with zero core edits
rungs.done_when: The three seams open, and two numbers exist: RMSE at fixed wall-clock time, and the cost of price plus all sensitivities over the cost of price alone, single digit and flat in the number of sensitivities.

rungs.title: Probability
items: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, Ch 1–4, with the Harvard Stat 110 lectures
Then Ch 5–10, most of the book; Ch 9 takes the longest
rungs.done_when: Bayes applied cold in an unfamiliar setup on paper, and any Mosteller problem solved cold.

rungs.title: Floating point
items: Goldberg, What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic, before the harness tolerance is chosen
Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, Ch 1–2
Kahan and pairwise summation against naive over ten million terms; -ffast-math sub-flag by sub-flag; FMA and reassociation
rungs.done_when: The harness tolerance chosen and defended, and why a stable algorithm on an ill-conditioned problem still fails.

rungs.title: Linear algebra
items: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra: covariance and the Cholesky decomposition, with MIT 18.06
rungs.done_when: What the eigenvalues of a covariance matrix mean, and what Cholesky is for.

rungs.title: Practice
rungs.because: After Blitzstein & Hwang Ch 3, because the problems assume conditioning and random variables.
items: Mosteller, Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability, alternating with Winkler, Mathematical Puzzles
Chen & Ankenman, The Mathematics of Poker, Part I and the toy games, argued aloud on paper
Crack, Heard on the Street, quantitative sections, twice

capabilities.name: Performance engineering
capabilities.goal: Know why code is fast or slow, and prove it with your own measurements.
capabilities.why: Speed is something you measure, not guess. A working model of the machine turns "why is this slow?" into a question with an answer.
capabilities.now: CSAPP Ch 2, deep on §2.4 floating point.
capabilities.gate: Every measurement in rungs 1–4 done on both machines, from programs you wrote, with the difference between the machines explained for each.
continuous: Muratori, Performance-Aware Programming: one section with its homework each week
Berger, Performance Matters, on measurement bias, in support of the variance rule

rungs.title: A model and the instruments
rungs.because: First, because prediction needs a model and the labs need instruments.
items: CSAPP Ch 1; §2.4 floating point; the rest of Ch 2 for integers and overflow
Algorithmica: the RAM-model and cache-hierarchy articles
Bakhvalov, Performance Analysis and Tuning on Modern CPUs, Part 1 Ch 1–6: perf, flamegraphs, top-down analysis
rungs.done_when: The pricer's per-path loop profiled on both machines (perf on the 9800X3D, Instruments on the M1 Max), and you can say where its time goes on each and why they differ.

rungs.title: The instruction level
rungs.because: After rung 1, because the bomb lab needs the instruments.
items: CSAPP Ch 3 in full, with the bomb lab
CSAPP Ch 5
Carruth, Understanding Compiler Optimization
A data-dependent branch timed over sorted then shuffled input, on both machines: the gap is the mispredict cost
rungs.done_when: The bomb lab done, and the mispredict cost measured on both machines with the difference explained.

rungs.title: The memory hierarchy
rungs.because: After rung 2, because cache effects are only attributable to a loop once you can read the loop.
items: CSAPP Ch 6, with the cache lab
Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, §3
Fog, Optimizing Software in C++, §7–9; Hennessy & Patterson Ch 2; Acton, Data-Oriented Design and C++; MIT 6.172 L1
Four programs: TLB reach, huge-page delta (9800X3D only), page-fault cost, sustained bandwidth
rungs.done_when: The cache lab done and the four programs run, with each difference between the machines explained.

rungs.title: Vectorisation and the OS boundary
rungs.because: After rung 3, because it needs the memory model.
items: Fog §12, vector operations; Doumler, Want Fast C++? Know Your Hardware
Auto-vectorisation failures read from the compiler's own reports: aliasing, restrict, alignment, trip counts
Two programs: syscall cost, and context-switch cost through a pipe
rungs.done_when: A loop of your own vectorised, why it previously wasn't stated from the report, and both programs run with the machines' difference explained.

capabilities.name: Concurrency and memory models
capabilities.goal: Understand memory ordering well enough to write concurrent code without guessing.
capabilities.why: Concurrent code that looks right is often wrong. Knowing what the memory model actually guarantees is the only way to write it without guessing.
capabilities.now: Not started. Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action, Ch 5 first.
capabilities.method: This ladder is a genuine dependency chain.

rungs.title: Correctness
items: Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action, Ch 5
ThreadSanitizer in CI from the first thread
rungs.done_when: Happens-before and the six orderings explained without notes.

rungs.title: Why the orderings exist
items: Sorin, Hill & Wood, A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, Ch 1–5
Sutter, atomic<> Weapons, both parts
rungs.done_when: Why x86 and ARM differ, in terms of the hardware.

rungs.title: Formal models and litmus tests
rungs.because: The tests mean nothing without rung 2.
items: Sewell et al., x86-TSO
ARM's barrier litmus test cookbook
SB, MP, LB and IRIW by hand, then under herd7 and litmus7
Preshing's articles, now and not before
rungs.done_when: A litmus outcome observed on the M1 Max that the 9800X3D can't produce, with the mechanism explained.

rungs.title: Coherence in practice
rungs.because: Needs the instruments from performance rung 1.
items: Per-thread counters packed into one array so they share cache lines: measured, attributed with a profiler, padded apart, re-measured, then contrasted with one shared counter
rungs.done_when: Before-and-after numbers with variance, and the attribution written.

rungs.title: The SPSC queue
items: Williams Ch 6, then Ch 7
A mutex-based queue first, then lock-free, benchmarked against each other with variance
The happens-before argument for the lock-free version, longhand
Every ordering classified as load-bearing or not, with what the weaker one would break
rungs.done_when: The argument holds, and the benchmark shows what lock-free actually bought.

capabilities.name: Software design
capabilities.goal: Taste in software design: structuring for clarity and simplicity, and modelling a problem well.
capabilities.why: Clear structure is what lets code keep changing. Small, timed builds train the instinct for where the boundaries go.
capabilities.now: Kernighan & Pike, and the next microapplication in your order.
capabilities.method: Microapplications, where design taste is actually built. Read the initial spec only, implement in 15–20 minutes, then extensions in 10–15, 15–20 and 20–25. No AI, and never a duplicate of a live project. The extensions are the point: each lands on a boundary you committed to before you knew it was coming, and which ones bend cheaply and which have to be torn out is the lesson.

rungs.title: The small scale
rungs.because: First, because it is language-light and pays off on the next thing you write.
items: Kernighan & Pike, The Practice of Programming, the whole book with notes
Microapplications 1–10
rungs.done_when: The book finished with notes, and ten microapplications shipped.

rungs.title: The module scale
rungs.because: After rung 1, because the microapplication extensions give you the failures Ousterhout names. Read him once you've felt them.
items: Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design
Microapplications 11–20
A written page per pricer seam as each is cut: what varies behind it, what the boundary cost. The seams are cut at pricer step 3, so this rung finishes after it
rungs.done_when: Ousterhout finished, twenty microapplications shipped, and the three seam pages written.

rungs.title: QuantLib, against the pricer
rungs.because: After rung 2, because without the vocabulary this is sightseeing.
items: Six questions, each traced in QuantLib and answered for your pricer, with the constraint that makes each the right choice
Instrument and PricingEngine; the Monte Carlo framework; how payoffs compose; curve bootstrapping; volatility surfaces; where the genericity actually lives
rungs.done_when: Six pages written and reviewed.

capabilities.name: Systems and low-latency architecture
capabilities.goal: Understand how a real low-latency system is built, end to end, well enough to design one yourself.
capabilities.why: Where every other capability meets: how a real low-latency system is built end to end, from the wire to the decision.
capabilities.now: Not started. Three lines; only the Disruptor paper depends on another line.
capabilities.gate: On a whiteboard: the path from wire to order book, every data structure choice and the alternative you rejected, and what you'd measure at each stage and roughly what the number should be.

rungs.title: The machine and the OS
rungs.because: In order.
items: CSAPP Ch 9, virtual memory, with the malloc lab
Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, Ch 13–20, then 7–10, then 36
Bonwick, The Slab Allocator, and tcmalloc's design document, read against your own allocator
rungs.done_when: The malloc lab passes, and you can say what a production allocator does that yours doesn't.

rungs.title: The network path
rungs.because: In order.
items: Beej's Guide to Network Programming
Stevens, TCP/IP Illustrated Vol 1: TCP connection management and data flow only
One liburing program batching reads through io_uring
rungs.done_when: Walk the TCP state machine and say where latency hides between the NIC and user space.

rungs.title: Market structure
rungs.because: Any order. Needs no systems knowledge; commute reading.
items: Harris, Trading and Exchanges, Ch 1–6
CME's match algorithms, and NYSE Pillar's order types and priority rules
The LMAX Disruptor paper, after the machine-and-OS line
One page each from the primary reports: the Flash Crash of May 2010, GameStop in January 2021, the Treasury market in March 2020
rungs.done_when: The three pages written.

rungs.title: Alongside
rungs.because: After concurrency rung 5, because it needs a latency-sensitive program of your own.
items: The lock-free SPSC queue's round-trip latency distribution, re-measured with isolcpus, IRQ affinity and transparent huge pages changed one at a time
Gregg, Systems Performance, as reference, and bpftrace as the instrument
